tables.how: All 183 Bay Area homes with a skilled-nursing licence and a State financial report for 2024 or 2025. 'Owed by related parties' is the report's current and non-current related-party receivables; the net figure subtracts related-party payables. A home is on the list when the net amount is at least half of everything it owns and at least $3 million: 46 homes (44 investor-owned), $1,144,753,197 between them, the case's figure; 3 are in San Francisco ($63,356,816). The other 137 are listed so the group can be set against everyone else. The chain is the affiliated entity in the federal enrollment file of October 2026, reached through the State's facility crosswalk. To rebuild a chain's totals, add up its homes that have a report for the chain's latest year: PACS Group, 31 homes, revenue $738,370,949, net income $119,229,623, $436,030,162 owed by related parties (78% of what its homes own) in 2025. 14 chains have three or more homes here.
tables.limits: A balance owed by a related company is not a payment and not a loss. The usual reason is central cash management: a chain's home office collects each home's cash and pays its bills, and the home books what it is owed; not-for-profit senior communities pool money across campuses the same way. The balance can be repaid, and dealing with a related company is disclosed in these reports. The State file does not say which related company owes the money, and has no line for management fees or rent paid to a related landlord. Reports for 2023 to 2025 are as submitted, not yet audited by the State; a report period can be shorter than a year. No authority has made a finding on any balance listed. Chain membership is today's, so a home bought recently carries its previous owner's earlier results; the federal file names some chains after a person.

tables.how: Every California row of the federal Payroll-Based Journal daily file for 2025Q3 to 2026Q2 was added up by home (1,153 California homes with 90 or more days reported; 188 in the six Bay Area counties, all listed here): hours of registered nurses, licensed practical or vocational nurses and nurse aides, divided by the people in the home each day in the same file. The California middle is 4.25 hours and the lowest quarter is below 4.01; 51 Bay Area homes are in that quarter and 97 are below the middle. 22 homes reported at least one day with people in the home and no registered-nurse hours of any kind; the most is 98 days. The middle California home's weekend figure is 3.83 and its registered-nurse figure 0.50; the federal chain file's national averages are 3.9 hours in all, 3.4 at weekends and 0.7 for registered nurses. Homes with five or more such days come first, then the fewest hours. A home is named as its State financial report names it where the Medicare provider number ties the two records, with the payroll file's spelling beside it. State penalties are matched by State facility number and are blank where the home has no State financial report to match through.
tables.limits: Hours are what the home's payroll system reported; a missed upload shows as zero hours, so a run of no-nurse days can be a filing gap. Small homes swing more. Homes that care mainly for people with mental illness use other staff who are not counted here, and hospital-based units and continuing-care communities staff higher because of who they care for. Half of all homes are below the middle by definition. Nothing here measures whether a home met the State's nursing-hours standard, and nothing shows that anyone in a home was harmed.

tables.how: The State report says how much related parties owe each home but not who they are. Medicare's ownership file of 1 October 2026 lists the parties each home disclosed, so the 46 listed homes were looked up there by enrollment number: 45 have rows. Listed: every named company in any role (an ownership, security or mortgage interest, operational or managerial control, or the role the file prints as 'ADP of the SNF', which the download does not explain), and every person with an ownership, partnership, security or mortgage interest or the role of corporate officer or director. Left out: 287 rows for people named only as managers, governing-body members or other parties; 46 rows for companies with no name in the file. One party appears once for each role it holds at each home.
tables.limits: This is each home's own disclosure of who owns, finances or manages it, and it reaches well beyond related companies: banks that hold a security interest and outside accounting, pharmacy and consulting firms are disclosed here too, and they are not the home's affiliates. It does not say which of these parties owes the home money, how much, or on what terms: that is in the home's audited statements and its related-party disclosures to the State, which are not on disk. A name in this list is not shown to be the same person as anyone of that name elsewhere. Owning, lending to or managing a nursing home is ordinary business, and being listed is not an accusation.

tables.how: Every unit in the inspector general's yearly statistical charts, fiscal 2018 to 2025. California reported 186 convictions in 2018 and 43 in 2025, 20.9 and 2.5 for every $10 billion of Medicaid spending; it ranks 48 of 53 units on that measure in 2025. The five other States with the largest Medicaid spending in 2025 (New York, Texas, Pennsylvania, Florida, Ohio) have a middle figure of 20.8.
tables.limits: The inspector general notes that recoveries are amounts defendants are required to pay and may not be collected; one large case can dominate a year. A conviction counted this year can come from an investigation opened years earlier, and cases brought by federal prosecutors are not in these counts. A low count is a question about capacity and choices, not evidence about how much fraud exists, and the charts say nothing about nursing homes in particular.
